<strong>Dar la vuelta al núcleo.</strong: Flip the kernel. Convolution runs through the kernel backwards: $(-1, 0, 1)$ flipped is $(1, 0, -1)$. That is what the $n-k$ of the formula says.
<strong>Resultado.</strong> $f * g = (-4: Result. $f * g = (-4,\ -1,\ 3)$. Out of five numbers come three: with a kernel of 3 and no overhang, the output measures $5 - 3 + 1 = 3$. And notice the sign: negative where the signal rises and positive where it falls, because the flipped kernel subtracts what lies ahead.

Casi nadie da la vuelta al núcleo en la: Hardly anyone flips the kernel in practice. What image libraries and neural networks do is cross-correlation, which is the same thing without the flip. It makes no difference when the kernel is symmetric — a blur is — and it changes the sign when it is not, as with the edge one. And in a network it makes no difference at all, because the numbers of the kernel are learnt: if they needed flipping, it would learn them flipped. It is worth knowing so as not to go mad comparing formulas from different places.

That is why an edge filter and a derivative are the same thing.

Then you slide the kernel one step and repeat. Nothing more.

Eso explica de golpe por qué los filtros: That explains at a stroke why filters do what they do. A smoothing kernel has a transform that is almost 1 at low frequencies and almost 0 at high ones: on multiplying, it lets the slow through and erases the fast, which is precisely the noise. That is why it is called a low-pass filter. And the derivative kernel does the opposite: it kills the low ones and amplifies the high ones.

La palabra alemana original era <em>Falt: The original German word was Faltung, “folding”, after that flip given to the kernel, and the English term convolution did not take hold until the thirties. The operation already appears in work by d'Alembert and Laplace on series, in the eighteenth century. What made it an everyday tool was the fast Fourier transform algorithm that Cooley and Tukey published in 1965: with it, the convolution theorem stopped being a theoretical curiosity and became the normal way of filtering anything.

Que se pueda hacer con una multiplicació: That it can be done with a multiplication has very practical consequences. An audio reverberation is the convolution of the sound with the response of a hall — a click is recorded in a cathedral and from then on any recording can sound as if it were there — and it is computed by Fourier because doing it directly would not run in real time. The same goes for the blur of your phone's photos, for cleaning up the curves of an epidemic and for telescopes, which recover the real image by undoing the convolution the atmosphere introduces. And the first layer of a network that looks at images is this operation with the numbers of the kernel learnt instead of chosen by hand.

Read as: “f convolved with g at row i, column j, is the double sum over u and v of f of i minus u, j minus v, times g of u, v”.

It is the same formula as before with one more index. And the size of the output follows the same rule: with an image of $H \times W$ and a kernel of $k \times k$, with no overhang, out come $(H - k + 1) \times (W - k + 1)$ pixels.
Se lee: <em>«efe convolucionada con ge,:
Read as: “f convolved with g, at position n, is the sum over k of f of n minus k times g of k”. The asterisk $*$ is the symbol of convolution, and it has nothing to do with multiplication.

Notice the $n - k$: the kernel is run through backwards with respect to the signal. That flip is what tells convolution apart from its sister correlation, which uses $n + k$, and it is explained further down.

The continuous version swaps the sum for an integral: $(f * g)(t) = \int f(t - s)\,g(s)\,ds$.
Se lee: <em>«la transformada de efe conv:
Read as: “the transform of f convolved with g is the transform of f times the transform of g”. The calligraphic $\mathcal{F}$ is “the Fourier transform of”.

In plain words: convolving in time is multiplying in frequency. The complicated operation becomes a number-by-number product.
Si los pesos <strong>suman 0</strong>, e: If the weights add up to 0, the filter is a difference: it detects changes, and leaves the smooth stretches at zero.
Si los pesos del núcleo <strong>suman 1<: If the weights of the kernel add up to 1, the filter is an average: it smooths, and leaves the smooth stretches as they were.
Si los pesos suman 1, el filtro suaviza: If the weights add up to 1, the filter smooths and keeps the level. If they add up to 0, it detects changes and leaves the smooth parts at zero.
Sobre una imagen, el núcleo pasa de ser: On an image, the kernel goes from being a list to being a small table, usually $3\times 3$, and instead of sliding along it slides by rows and columns. At each position the nine numbers are multiplied by the nine pixels beneath and added. The earlier rule still holds word for word: if the weights add up to 1 it blurs, and if they add up to 0 it brings out the edges.
Suavizar una curva de contagios, desenfo: Smoothing an infection curve, blurring a photo, finding the edges of an image, adding reverberation to a sound and the first layer of a network that recognises digits are, on the inside, the same computation: sliding a small list of numbers over a large list, multiplying and adding at each position. That small list is called a kernel, and what the filter does depends only on what numbers it has.

Y ahora la conexión con [[av-fourier|Fou: And now the connection with [[av-fourier|Fourier]], which is the result that makes convolution a big idea and not just a programming trick. Convolving two signals is a long computation: with a signal of $n$ numbers and a kernel of $m$, it costs on the order of $n\cdot m$ multiplications. But in the world of frequencies it becomes something ridiculously simple.
